slides.title: Two individually valid objects can be a bad pair
keyPoints: A sender writes one digit
A receiver reads that representation
The decoded value must equal the original
slides.narration: A sender and receiver can each look correct on their own and still fail together. Our teaching protocol has ten possible values, zero through nine. One family writes a bare digit such as 7. Another writes a framed digit such as [7]. The receiving object must understand the same family that the sending object used. We are not sending a real network message; the wire in this chapter is a string passed between functions. That small model lets us inspect every accepted value. The key problem is agreement between two products. It will lead us to select a whole family instead of making two unrelated choices.
actions: Ask learners to decode 7 and [7] under each proposed rule.
Write the round-trip promise in words before introducing factory names.

question.prompt: What is the central promise connecting encoder and decoder?
question.answer: For every allowed digit, reading the string produced by the matching encoder must return the original value.

slides.title: Treat compatibility as an explicit requirement
keyPoints: Numbers outside 0–9 are rejected
Shape and digit content are both checked
Cross-family input must not silently pass
slides.narration: An encoder turns a value into a representation. A decoder turns that representation back into a value. Those names tell us their jobs but do not prove they agree. Our requirements include positive cases and rejection cases: all ten digits must round-trip, an out-of-range integer must fail, and malformed text must fail. Framing also has two parts. The brackets must be right, and the middle character must be a decimal digit. A string like [x] has the right shape and the wrong content. Writing these checks before choosing the design helps us catch a family assembled from the wrong members later.
actions: Build a small accepted/rejected table for 0, 9, 10, [7], and [x].
Ask which tests are about numeric range and which are about representation.

question.prompt: Why is accepting [x] a defect even though its brackets are correct?
question.answer: The frame is structurally valid, but the contained character is outside the digit protocol. Both conditions are required.

slides.title: A single protocol starts with two functions
keyPoints: No factory is needed for one fixed pair
A colon introduces each value from the list
Subtracting character 0 gives the checked digit value
slides.narration: The simplest version uses two ordinary functions. The loop's colon means take each value from the list on the right and run the body with that value. Each iteration writes a digit, then reads it back. std::to_string produces text; it does not change the integer into a character by casting. In the reader, we first require exactly one decimal digit. Only then do we subtract the character '0'. Decimal digit characters are consecutive in C++, so this gives the numeric value after the range check. The three printed lines demonstrate normal behavior for the chosen inputs. They do not replace the exhaustive ten-value check in the chapter program.

question.prompt: Why does read_digit subtract the character 0 rather than the integer zero?
question.answer: The input is an encoded character. Subtracting the code for character 0 converts a validated decimal character to its numeric value.

slides.title: A mismatch can compile and still fail at the boundary
keyPoints: Framed output is a valid string
Plain input requires exactly one digit
Type agreement does not imply protocol agreement
slides.narration: This sender produces [4], and the receiver expects exactly one character. There is no C++ type error: the sender returns std::string and the reader accepts a string reference. Execution rejects the three-character input. The final control call shows the reader can handle its own valid input, so blaming all decoding would be too broad. The defect is the pair selected during setup. This same problem occurs when a serializer and parser disagree about a version or when a user-interface family mixes incompatible parts. Abstract Factory will move family selection into one object. It reduces opportunities for mismatches, but we will still need behavioral tests.
actions: Predict whether the error is at build time or run time.
Run and use the final control line to narrow the diagnosis.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Round-trip every digit from 0 through 9 in either family.
Reject numbers outside the supported range and malformed wire strings.
Create both products from one selected factory and own them locally.
slides.narration:
Plain and framed digit codec families. CodecFactory groups two independent creation operations under one family choice. round_trip depends only on factory and product interfaces, and explicitly checks the compatibility invariant.

Round-trip every digit from 0 through 9 in either family. Reject numbers outside the supported range and malformed wire strings. Create both products from one selected factory and own them locally.

For each supported digit, read(write(value)) equals value within one family. Products returned by the supplied factories are non-null. Decoders check structure before indexing or extracting content. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. A single Codec type with write and read methods avoids pairing entirely if send and receive need not be separate objects. A simple function returning an owning pair is also sufficient for a small closed set of families.

slides.narration:
A small teaching protocol transmits one decimal digit, from 0 through 9. A plain connection sends 7 as the string 7. A framed connection sends the same value as [7]. Each connection needs two objects: an encoder that writes a digit and a decoder that reads the resulting string. Every accepted digit must survive the trip unchanged. Invalid numbers and malformed strings must be rejected.

Constructing a PlainEncoder and PlainDecoder directly is enough for the first version. They have separate jobs, and their relationship is easy to see. The excerpt is a complete sequence of statements inside a caller, assuming the two types are available. It does not need a factory for its own sake.

slides.title: The failure is a mismatched pair
keyPoints: When framed connections arrive, setup code selects both products independently.
A family is a set of objects meant to work together.
slides.narration:
When framed connections arrive, setup code selects both products independently. A copied branch can create FramedEncoder with PlainDecoder. Both objects implement the right C++ interfaces, so the compiler accepts the code. The encoder produces [7], but the plain decoder rejects its length. A more permissive decoder might silently misread the data instead. The problem is agreement between products, not merely selecting one product.

A family is a set of objects meant to work together. The Abstract Factory pattern gives the caller one object that creates all needed members of the selected family. CodecFactory offers encoder and decoder. PlainFactory creates the plain pair; FramedFactory creates the framed pair. The client chooses one factory, then asks that factory for both products. This reduces the number of places where incompatible choices can enter.

slides.title: Two product roles are not one inheritance tree
keyPoints: Encoder and Decoder have different operations, so they remain different interfaces.
The factory itself is borrowed as const CodecFactory&.
The compiler checks product method signatures and factory overrides.
slides.narration:
Encoder and Decoder have different operations, so they remain different interfaces. PlainEncoder and FramedEncoder implement Encoder. PlainDecoder and FramedDecoder implement Decoder. Each concrete factory creates one of each. Abstract Factory does not require these two products to inherit from each other, share a common catch-all interface, or own one another. Their useful relationship is a protocol contract: decoder.read(encoder.write(value)) equals value for every valid value.

The factory itself is borrowed as const CodecFactory&. The client does not delete it and does not save its address. Each returned unique_ptr owns a fresh product. The products contain no reference back to the factory, so this implementation does not require them to die before the factory. In round_trip they are local and are destroyed when the call ends. A different implementation with shared factory state would need a documented lifetime rule instead of assuming this one applies.

The compiler checks product method signatures and factory overrides. During execution, the actual factory type chooses the concrete products. Calling through Encoder and Decoder then chooses their actual method implementations. The client contains no switch on wire format. It still knows the abstract protocol duties: one writer, one reader, a valid integer, and a round-trip invariant.

slides.title: Parsing is part of the contract
keyPoints: PlainDecoder checks that wire has exactly one character before testing its content.
The character tests compare the input with '0' and '9'.
The encoder checks numeric range before making a string.
slides.narration:
PlainDecoder checks that wire has exactly one character before testing its content. The || operator stops as soon as an operand is true. This short-circuit rule skips unnecessary content tests after a bad length. FramedDecoder uses the same ordering for a stronger safety reason: front() and back() require a nonempty string. Its size check rejects empty input before either operation can run. C++17 permits reading string[string.size()] as a zero character, so PlainDecoder’s wire[0] on an empty string is not the same invalid-access case as front() or back().

The character tests compare the input with '0' and '9'. C++ guarantees the decimal digit characters form a consecutive sequence, so subtracting '0' from a checked digit yields its numeric value. The framed reader first checks a three-character shape with opening and closing brackets. Only then does it take the one-character substring and reuse PlainDecoder. That reuse is a local parsing dependency, not membership in the plain factory family.

The encoder checks numeric range before making a string. The framed decoder rejects [x] even though its outer brackets are correct. Structural validity and content validity are different rules. These deliberately tiny formats let the tests cover all ten accepted numeric values. They are teaching protocols, not general-purpose serialization formats with escaping, byte-order rules, versioning, or checksums.

slides.title: A factory encourages compatibility; it does not prove it
keyPoints: Nothing in the return types prevents a faulty FramedFactory from returning PlainDecoder.
A factory is most useful when clients need several related product roles and whole families change together.
For one encoder-decoder pair with no planned variants, direct construction is clearer.
slides.narration:
Nothing in the return types prevents a faulty FramedFactory from returning PlainDecoder. The family rule is a design contract backed by tests. round_trip checks the value after decoding. That catches mismatches or broken decoding for the tested values. It cannot certify all future protocol extensions by itself. If a family has many configuration values, test representative boundaries and generated cases, and consider carrying a shared immutable configuration object into both products.

A factory is most useful when clients need several related product roles and whole families change together. Adding a new family is local: provide its products and a factory implementing the existing creation operations. Adding a new product role is less local: a new creation method affects every factory and every family. This is the pattern’s main change-direction tradeoff. Choose it when new families are more likely than new roles.

For one encoder-decoder pair with no planned variants, direct construction is clearer. A function returning a struct containing both owning handles can also preserve pairing with less inheritance. Compile-time family types or a single codec object can enforce stronger relationships when runtime variation is unnecessary. Do not split one naturally cohesive codec into separate products solely to make an Abstract Factory diagram. Here separate send and receive components are the stated need; the factory coordinates their creation.

slides.title: Choose the family once, then ask for its members
keyPoints: CodecFactory offers encoder and decoder
Each concrete factory supplies one matching family
The client depends on product roles
slides.narration: A family is a set of objects intended to work together. CodecFactory declares two creation operations because the client needs two product roles: an encoder and a decoder. PlainFactory supplies the plain members, while FramedFactory supplies the framed members. round_trip receives one factory and asks that same factory for both products. It does not select an encoder from one source and a decoder from an unrelated source. This is the organizing idea of Abstract Factory. The client still knows what sending and receiving mean. It simply stops naming the concrete format classes. New family choices can then be made at setup without scattering those names through the protocol workflow.

theory.why: Independent setup choices can mix incompatible protocol members.

slides.title: Separate product roles keep the interface honest
keyPoints: Encoder writes; Decoder reads
Neither product is a subtype of the other
Compatibility is a relationship between behaviors
slides.narration: A decoder is not a special kind of encoder. Giving them a common do_everything interface would hide their different duties. In the chapter, each role has its own base class and virtual operation. The plain and framed encoders share Encoder; the plain and framed decoders share Decoder. Factories create across these two hierarchies. This distinction helps us read the UML: inheritance arrows stay within a role, while creation dependencies connect a factory to its concrete products. The compatibility rule sits across the pair: read after write returns the original allowed value. That rule is not an inheritance arrow and is not proved by making the products share a base class.
actions: Name the operation on each product interface.
Explain why the pair contract belongs in tests as well as documentation.

question.prompt: Would inheriting Decoder from Encoder enforce a matching protocol?
question.answer: No. It confuses distinct roles and says nothing about whether read and write agree on their representations.

slides.title: A borrowed factory can create owned products
keyPoints: const CodecFactory& borrows configuration choice
Local unique_ptr values own the products
This implementation stores no back-pointer to the factory
slides.narration: The reference parameter lets round_trip use a factory that remains owned by its caller. const stops the client from calling non-const factory operations through that parameter. The products are different: each returned unique_ptr gives round_trip responsibility for one object's cleanup. If the second creation throws, the first local owner is still destroyed as the function exits through the exception. The concrete products here do not refer back to their factory, so their behavior does not require keeping the factory alive. That conclusion follows from this source code, not from the pattern name. A future factory that lends shared configuration to products would need an explicit lifetime rule.
actions: Mark the borrowed parameter and the two owning local variables.
Ask how storing a factory reference inside a product would change the contract.

question.prompt: If decoder creation throws after encoder creation succeeded, who releases the encoder?
question.answer: The encoder local unique_ptr releases it during exception cleanup. The borrowed factory remains the caller’s responsibility.

slides.title: Guard the shape before reading its parts
keyPoints: Check wire size first
Only then inspect brackets and the middle digit
Shape validation and value validation are separate
slides.narration: The framed reader checks for length three before calling front or back. The logical-or operator, written as two vertical bars, stops when one condition is already true. If the size is wrong, the later bracket checks do not run. This matters because front and back require a nonempty string. Once the three-character shape and brackets are confirmed, the reader extracts the middle character and reuses the plain digit reader. That is a local parsing dependency, not evidence that the framed decoder belongs to the plain factory family. A parser must reject both missing structure and invalid content. Testing only [7] would miss [x], an empty string, or extra trailing text.
actions: Trace the guard for an empty string and then for [x].
Ask which layer rejects each input and why.

question.prompt: Why must the size check appear before front and back in this guard?
question.answer: Short-circuit evaluation skips those operations for an invalid length, including empty input where front and back would be unsafe.

slides.title: The factory promises compatibility; tests check it
keyPoints: Override checks signatures
Return types do not encode the family pairing
Exhaust all ten valid values and test malformed input
slides.narration: Suppose FramedFactory accidentally returns PlainDecoder from decoder. That return can satisfy unique_ptr<Decoder>, and the override can compile perfectly. The family contract is still broken. This is why the chapter's round_trip checks the decoded result, and why main exercises all ten valid values. A successful round-trip for one value may miss a reader that mishandles another digit. Rejection tests add different evidence: inputs from the wrong family and malformed strings must fail as promised. In a larger protocol, complete enumeration may be impossible, so boundary tests and generated cases matter. The pattern organizes responsibility; it does not turn behavioral promises into automatic mathematical proof.
actions: Propose the faulty factory change verbally and classify whether it compiles.
Ask why all valid digits still matter after one mismatch test.

question.prompt: What test exposes a framed factory that returns a plain decoder?
question.answer: Request both products from that factory and round-trip a valid digit such as 7. The plain decoder rejects the framed string.

slides.narration:
Abstract Factory coordinates creation of related products. Product interfaces describe roles; family contracts describe compatibility. Use the same selected factory for all members of a family. Adding a family is easier than adding a new product role. Round-trip tests reveal agreement that C++ signatures cannot prove.

Choose a family at the application boundary and pass that choice inward. New transport variants can then reuse the round-trip workflow and its checks instead of adding independent switches throughout the code.

question.prompt: Explain Abstract Factory without reciting its class names.
question.answer: CodecFactory groups two independent creation operations under one family choice. round_trip depends only on factory and product interfaces, and explicitly checks the compatibility invariant. A single Codec type with write and read methods avoids pairing entirely if send and receive need not be separate objects. A simple function returning an owning pair is also sufficient for a small closed set of families.

slides.title: Expect cheap new families and expensive new roles
keyPoints: Adding a family implements existing creation operations
Adding a product role changes every factory
Choose the design for the likely change
slides.narration: Every abstraction favors some changes over others. Adding TaggedFactory is local because encoder and decoder are already the agreed roles. The new family supplies those two products while round_trip continues using the same interface. Adding a third role, such as a validator product, is a wider change if it becomes a required operation on CodecFactory. Every concrete factory must then decide what to return. This is a practical maintenance cost, not a flaw we can wish away. Before choosing Abstract Factory, ask whether you expect many new families of stable roles or frequent changes to the list of roles itself. A small bundle-returning function may be easier when the family set is fixed.

slides.title: Do not split a good codec merely to fit a diagram
keyPoints: One cohesive codec may be enough
A returned bundle can keep setup together
Compile-time families can provide stronger constraints
slides.narration: A design pattern should solve a real separation problem. If one object naturally owns both writing and reading, keeping a single codec may express the requirement more clearly. If separate objects are useful but no runtime family switching is needed, a function can return a struct containing a matched pair. When the family is known during compilation, distinct family types or templates can rule out some mismatches earlier. Abstract Factory is valuable here because separate send and receive products are required and clients select a family through a stable runtime interface. Choose deliberately. More interfaces do not automatically mean more safety; they can also create more places for a configuration mistake.

slides.title: Recall the contract, then reconstruct the architecture
keyPoints: One family selection supplies both roles
read(write(value)) equals value
Malformed and mixed-family representations are rejected
slides.narration: Try rebuilding the idea from the failure rather than from a class diagram. Independently chosen senders and receivers can disagree about string format. We therefore choose one family object and request both roles from it. The client owns the returned products and checks the same round-trip promise through their interfaces. Now imagine supporting a new tagged format d=7. Describe the new encoder, decoder, and factory, then list the old tests that must continue to pass. Finally, explain what the pattern cannot guarantee: a badly written factory can still return the wrong member, and the compiler may accept it. This final boundary is part of understanding the pattern, not a reason to skip it.
